intrinsic_value_estimate: About $80 per share as the central estimate, with a range of $56–100. Method: owner earnings, in line with brk-letter-1986, taken as a perpetuity in two stages. The base is 1988 owner earnings of about $2.60 per share (estimate range $2.45–2.75). That figure is net income of $2.85 plus depreciation, less maintenance capex assumed close to depreciation, excluding undistributed affiliate earnings. Central case: owner earnings grow 10% a year for 10 years, below the company's 13–14% record, then 5% a year forever, discounted at 10%. The 10% rate is a proxy based on the 10% average coupon on the company's own debt; no government bond yield is in the packet. Other cases: if the past simply repeats (13% growth), about $102; pessimistic growth (7%/4%), about $57; management's own 12% cost of capital, about $56 for the base case and about $42 for the pessimistic case. On top of this sit roughly $6 per share of CCE, CPE and other bottler stakes at carrying value. I credit only about $3 for them, as a cushion, and leave them out of the margin calculation. The 1965 net-working-capital test gives about $0 per share (net-net of about –$1.0B), but that test was superseded by brk-letter-1987#18.
margin_of_safety: At $46.56 (close on 1989-02-24), the margin of safety is about 42% against the $80 central value and about 54% if the past repeats. With lower terminal growth or the 12% discount rate it is about 17–27%. The margin is negative (–11%) only when pessimistic growth and the 12% rate are combined. The framework's test as of this date is a 'sensible price for an outstanding business' that holds up 'even should the future... develop much along the lines of its past' (brk-letter-1981#3). That test is passed with room to spare. Cross-check: at 12% growth, the earnings yield on today's price reaches about 10.8% in five years and keeps rising, above the company's own bond coupons.

key_reasons.reason: The business earns high returns on equity without relying on leverage. The core business earns far more than the consolidated figures show.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Business analysis: return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE was 19.4–21.2% every year from 1976 to 1983, with debt at only 3.5–17% of capital (ar-1986 selected data). It was 27.2% in 1987 and 33% in 1988 (upi-1989-01-31). Soft-drink operating income on identifiable assets was about 34–36% pretax, and about 52% for International in 1987 (ar-1987 note 16).

key_reasons.reason: The moat is wide and getting wider. Pricing power shows in rising margins, record share, and a quick recovery from the 1985 formula change.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Business analysis: durable competitive advantage, the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16); strong franchises keep corporate tax cuts as profit (brk-letter-1986#22)
key_reasons.evidence: Gross margin on concentrate is about 63% (ar-1986). Consolidated gross margin rose from 50.5% to about 55% between 1985 and 1988 while the statutory tax rate fell from 46% to 34%. US share is over 40%, the fountain lead is more than 2-to-1, and worldwide share is about 44% (ar-1987, upi-1989-01-31). Classic became the #1 US soft drink in 1986, a year after New Coke.

key_reasons.reason: Growth needs little capital and has a long way to run. Owner earnings are close to reported earnings.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Business analysis: owner earnings (brk-letter-1986); contrast with capital-hungry commodity businesses (brk-letter-1985#9)
key_reasons.evidence: 1987 soft-drink capex was about $170M against about $1.43B of soft-drink operating income (ar-1987). International consumption per person is 16% of the US rate (ar-1986). Estimated 1987 owner earnings are about $660–805M against $916M of net income.

key_reasons.reason: Management passes the $1-retained test by a wide margin. They have shrunk the share count at sensible prices and are refocusing the company on its core business.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Management & capital allocation: each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983); buybacks below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1984)
key_reasons.evidence: From 1981 to 1988, about $6.46 per share was retained and the share price rose from $11.13 to $46.56, about $5.50 of market value per $1 retained (about $2.60 assuming no rise in the P/E multiple). About 69M shares were repurchased from 1984 to 1988, mostly at 11–15x earnings (ar-1986, ar-1987, upi-1989-01-31). Entertainment was spun into CPE and soft drinks now make up more than 95% of operating income.

key_reasons.reason: The price is sensible against conservatively estimated value. The stock doesn't need to be a Graham bargain.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Valuation as of 1989: 'an outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre business at a bargain price' (brk-letter-1987#18), superseding the net-working-capital rule (bpl-letter-1965); price must make sense if the future resembles the past (brk-letter-1981#3)
key_reasons.evidence: The price of $46.56 is 16.3x 1988 EPS of $2.85, with an owner-earnings yield of about 5.6% and growth of about 11–14% a year over the record (prices, upi-1989-01-31). Central intrinsic value is about $80, a margin of about 42%.

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst is needed. Value compounds through earnings growth and the share buyback already in progress. The market multiple has not expanded.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Catalyst/timing: the market eventually confirms business success; Mr. Market is there to serve, not guide (brk-letter-1987); no market forecasting (bpl-letter-1966-mid)
key_reasons.evidence: The P/E was about 15.7x at end-1987 ($38.13/$2.43) and about 16.3x now. About 14.5M shares remain in the 40M-share buyback program through 1990 (upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: A concentrated position is justified: the facts are clear and a drastic loss of value is unlikely. I hold below the 40% maximum because of the gaps in the information.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Position sizing: up to 40% of net worth when there is an extremely high probability that the facts are correct and a very low probability of drastic change (bpl-letter-1965); hunting elephants (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: A century-old franchise that survived its own 1985 blunder, with a market cap of about $16.5B and earnings of about $1.04B, so it is large enough to matter. The 1988 cash-flow statement is missing, and 74% of operating income is exposed to currency (ar-1987).

risks: Currency: about 74% of operating income comes from outside the US. Hard currencies strengthened 27%, 16% and 10% in 1986–88, which flattered reported growth, and a reversal would slow it.
Owner earnings are estimated. With no 1988 cash-flow statement, if maintenance capex is closer to total capex, owner earnings fall to about $2.30 and value falls about 12%.
Discount rate: no government bond yield is in the packet. At management's 12% rate combined with pessimistic growth, value (about $42) is below the price.
About $1.8–2.2B of capital sits in low-return affiliates (CCE about 6% on net assets; CPE had write-downs in 1988), and more capital could go into them.

Management's appetite for debt: the net debt-to-capital ceiling was raised to 35% and short-term debt reached $1.7B at end-1987 to fund buybacks and bottler stakes. The framework prefers little or no debt.
Formula-pricing contracts with most US bottlers limit US pricing freedom outside CCE.
Hyperinflation and low margins in Latin America; the Foods business is declining (orange juice volumes fell 22% for frozen and 6% for chilled in 1988).
Off-balance-sheet guarantees of about $394M and recourse on about $325M of CPE receivables.
Management's character and owner-orientation haven't been tested in person, and promotional reporting is a mild warning sign on candor.
what_would_change_my_mind: If the 1988 10-K shows maintenance capex well above depreciation, so owner earnings are materially below about $2.45 per share.
If growth with currency effects removed turns out to be in the low single digits, which would mean the record was mostly translation gains.
If long-term government bond yields are well above 10%, so the price fails the sensible-price test.
If meeting management shows they are not owner-oriented: buybacks without regard to value, compensation unconnected to returns on capital, or appetite for another diversification like Columbia.
If the price rises to around or above the central value of about $80 with no change in the business, the margin of safety disappears and I would stop adding (but not necessarily sell).
If the price falls sharply while the business holds up, I would add toward the 35–40% cap.
sell_triggers: The franchise erodes: sustained loss of US or worldwide share to the main competitor, or gross margins falling for several years without a temporary cause.

Management turns to value-destroying diversification or issues shares worth less than they cost owners (brk-letter-1982#17), such as a large acquisition outside soft drinks or another Columbia-style move.
Leverage rises well beyond the 35% net debt-to-capital ceiling to fund buybacks or affiliates, making this a business that needs debt.

Evidence that I misread the basic economics (brk-letter-1987#18), for example if the core concentrate returns of about 34–36% pretax turn out to depend on bottler subsidies or accounting moved off the balance sheet.
Not a trigger: a high stock price on its own. The default for a great business with able managers is to hold it permanently (brk-letter-1987#18; brk-letter-1983#2).
